paragraphs.title: The Prophet Exposes the Gap Between External Fasting and True Change

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet.”
easy.q: How is the prophet commanded to lift up his voice?

easy.explanation: He is commanded to show Israel their transgression and the house of Jacob their sins.
easy.q: What is the prophet to show the people?

answers: Why have we fasted, and thou seest not?
easy.explanation: They ask, “Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not?”
easy.q: What question did the people ask about their fasting?

answers: Between religious appearance and oppressive conduct
medium.explanation: The people appeared eager to seek God, yet they pursued their own pleasures and oppressed others.
medium.q: What contrast does the prophet expose?

medium.explanation: The people fasted while still exacting or demanding labor from others.
medium.q: In the KJV, what does “exact all your labours” mean in context?

answers: Because the fast is too short
Because their conduct has not changed
Because fasting is forbidden on that day
medium.explanation: Their fasting is accompanied by pleasure-seeking, strife, debate, and violence.
medium.q: Why is bodily suffering alone not an acceptable fast?

answers: Bowing the head and spreading sackcloth and ashes
Eating bread and satisfying the hungry
challenge.explanation: Bowing the head and wearing sackcloth and ashes are outward signs without the required moral change.
challenge.q: Which detail shows the people focused on outward signs of fasting?

answers: Fasting does not correct immoral behavior
challenge.explanation: The passage places religious suffering beside strife and violence to show that outward fasting alone is ineffective.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the movement from fasting to fighting and violence?

answers: The people wanted their fast to gain God’s attention
challenge.explanation: They wanted their fasting to be noticed by God, but their conduct made the ritual unacceptable.
challenge.q: What does “to make your voice to be heard on high” suggest in context?

paragraphs.title: The Desired Fast: Justice, Compassion, and Care for the Needy

easy.explanation: The passage says, “let the oppressed go free.”
easy.q: What is one part of the fast God has chosen?

easy.explanation: The desired fast includes dealing bread to the hungry.
easy.q: What should be given to the hungry?

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him.”
easy.q: What should be done when someone is naked?

answers: Freeing the oppressed, feeding the hungry, and clothing the naked
Bowing the head, wearing sackcloth, and fighting
medium.explanation: The passage describes practical mercy and justice rather than merely outward mourning.
medium.q: Which sequence correctly describes the desired fast?

medium.explanation: The phrase calls for removing the restraints and injustices that oppress people.
medium.q: What does “to loose the bands of wickedness” mean?

medium.explanation: Both actions move from outward ritual to practical help for those in need.
medium.q: What do breaking burdens and bringing the poor into the house have in common?

answers: A person must not ignore relatives and others in need
A person should leave his family
challenge.explanation: The phrase emphasizes personal responsibility toward one’s own people and those who need help.
challenge.q: What does “hide not thyself from thine own flesh” teach about helping the needy?

answers: Breaking every yoke and freeing the oppressed
challenge.explanation: Breaking yokes and freeing the oppressed directly correct unjust conditions.
challenge.q: Which action most clearly shows the move from bodily affliction to justice?

answers: It addresses hunger, poverty, nakedness, and oppression
challenge.explanation: The commands focus on meeting the concrete needs of other people.
challenge.q: Why does the desired fast include social responsibility?

paragraphs.title: The Blessings of Justice: Light, Healing, Guidance, and Restoration

easy.explanation: The passage says, “Then shall thy light break forth as the morning.”
easy.q: What will break forth for the person who acts rightly?

answers: The one who hides the poor
The one who calls upon Him and turns from oppression
The one who strikes with wickedness
easy.explanation: The Lord promises, “Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall answer,” after describing righteous conduct.

answers: A watered garden and a spring of water
easy.explanation: The person is compared to “a watered garden” and “a spring of water, whose waters fail not.”
easy.q: What will the righteous person be like?

answers: Mourning, bowed heads, sackcloth, and debate
medium.explanation: The passage promises light, health, God’s answer, guidance, and satisfaction.
medium.q: Which sequence of blessings appears in these verses?

medium.explanation: The KJV word “health” refers to healing or restoration that comes quickly.
medium.q: In “thine health shall spring forth speedily,” what does “health” mean?

answers: By rebuilding waste places and restoring paths
medium.explanation: The people are described as rebuilding old waste places and restoring paths to dwell in.
medium.q: How does the righteous person become an agent of restoration?

answers: Both describe a movement from darkness to light
Both describe a time of fasting
challenge.explanation: The images portray God’s blessing as illumination overcoming darkness.
challenge.q: What relationship exists between the person’s light and his darkness becoming as noon?

answers: A continuing source of life and blessing
challenge.explanation: Unfailing waters suggest abundance, stability, and lasting refreshment.
challenge.q: What does the image of a spring whose waters fail not suggest?

answers: Justice includes restoring damaged communities and paths
challenge.explanation: The blessing extends beyond private renewal to the restoration of places and communities.
challenge.q: Why do the blessings include rebuilding ancient ruins?

paragraphs.title: Honoring the Sabbath and Receiving God’s Promise

easy.explanation: The passage says to turn away from doing one’s pleasure on God’s holy day.
easy.q: From what should a person turn his foot on the sabbath?

answers: As a delight and honorable holy day
As a day of suffering only
easy.explanation: The sabbath is called “a delight, the holy of the Lord, honourable.”
easy.q: How should the sabbath be regarded?

answers: Delight in the Lord and the heritage of Jacob
easy.explanation: The Lord promises delight, elevation, and the heritage of Jacob.
easy.q: What is promised to the person who honors the sabbath?

answers: Doing one’s pleasure, finding one’s pleasure, and speaking one’s words
Turning from one’s own ways, pleasure, and words
medium.explanation: The passage calls people to refrain from their own ways, pleasure, and words.
medium.q: Which sequence best describes honoring the sabbath?

medium.explanation: The sabbath is to be treated as a joyful and honored sacred day.
medium.q: What does “delight” mean in “call the sabbath a delight”?

answers: Honoring the sabbath is linked to delighting in the Lord and receiving His promise
Honoring the sabbath removes every blessing
medium.explanation: “Then” connects sabbath honor with the promised delight, elevation, and inheritance.
medium.q: What connects honoring the sabbath with the final blessing?

answers: Sabbath observance concerns conduct, activities, and speech
Only clothing matters on the sabbath
challenge.explanation: The verse names several areas of life, showing that sabbath honor is comprehensive.
challenge.q: What does the command to avoid one’s ways, pleasure, and words show?

challenge.explanation: The image expresses exaltation and blessing for those who honor the Lord.
challenge.q: What does riding upon the high places of the earth symbolize?

answers: With a prediction of continued strife
With “for the mouth of the Lord hath spoken it”
With a command to fast again
challenge.explanation: The final statement grounds the promise in the authoritative word of the Lord.
challenge.q: How does the passage end, and what confirms the promise?
